Abstract

The origin of viruses is ancient and the details are uncertain. Viruses may have preceded cellular life, may have arisen in parallel with cells, or maybe evolved from early cellular life forms. This chapter will explore the various hypotheses for viral origins and the evidence for and against each hypothesis. Lastly, the more recent co-evolution of viruses with humans and our hominid ancestors is discussed.

url_citation.content:
Micro- organisms are microscopic or submicroscopic (unable to be viewed with an ordinary microscope). Bacteria, protists, and fungi are microorganisms. There is disagreement in the scientific community, however, about whether viruses are actually living organisms and, therefore, can be considered microorganisms. Viruses do not fit into any of the generally accepted kingdoms of life. Although they have genes and can adapt to their environment, viruses cannot grow or reproduce outside a living host cell.

...

A virus is a microscopic particle (not a cell) that cannot grow or reproduce outside of a living cell. Viruses act as invaders, using their structure and chemical makeup to live and replicate at the cost of the host organism. Because they live off of and harm humans and other living organisms, viruses are considered parasites.
Viruses are extremely small; scientists must use a highly specialized electron microscope to view them. The core of a virus is made up of nucleic acid, either RNA or DNA. This genetic material directs the operations of the virus and is protected by a protein shell called a capsid.

...

Viruses are a major cause of disease. Some viruses, such as the one that causes the common cold, do not typically result in a grave illness. Others, however, such as those that cause Ebola and rabies in humans, are rarer and more deadly. Vaccines are a way to combat some viruses, such as mumps, measles, and chickenpox.
